newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Sky City in line with forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sky City in line with forecasts.

text.p: First half results from casino operator Sky City Ltd were broadly consistent with market forecasts and the mid-year opening of its Sky Tower will add a new earnings stream, analysts said on Monday.
Despite ongoing difficulties with peripheral services, there was little to change the company's medium to long-term prospects, they said.

Sky, half-owned by Brierley Investments and 12.5 percent by Harrah's Entertainment, earlier reported a six-month profit of NZ$18.2 million in the half year to December, up from $15.5 million in the six months to June 1996.
Sky City said it was still on track to achieve its full year forecast of NZ$35.8 million for the year to June 1997.
Chairman Jon Hartley said although the casino had been open for 12 months, the company was still learning how its customers responded to the business at different times of the year.

"That being said, thus far we are not noting significant variations in customer attendance over the seasons," he told a news briefing. "The challenge for management in the next period is to further increase gaming revenue whilst providing more popular offerings in non-gaming sectors and producing efficiencies on the cost side of the business," he said.

Sky Tower telecommunications contracts were being negotiated and conditional contracts agreed. Sky City expects 900,000 visitors to the tower a year. The tower will include a 180-seat revolving restaurant and observation decks.

Managing Director Evan Davies said progress in obtaining a casino licence for Queenstown in the South Island had been slower than envisaged, due in part to local opposition and "ongoing contemplation" by the Casino Control Authority as to the best way to deal with further applications.
Davies said about NZ$200,000 had been spent on the Queenstown proposal. In Wellington, Sky City was continuing to investigate appropriate casino locations.
Raymond Webb at ANZ Securities said the Sky City's win per day from patrons, at NZ$590,000, was strong, mostly due to the success of its slot machine business.
Webb estimated "other" operations lost about NZ$577,000 after direct costs over the six months, but he still expects a net profit overall result of around NZ$38 million for the year.
"We remain positive on the company in the medium term and long term, with earnings still to come on stream from the Sky Tower," he said.
"We believe that they will get the peripheral operations right and that will be positive for earnings going forward," he said.
Sky City said it was looking at development options for the site adjoining the existing Sky City complex.
Among the options is a combination of entertainment attractions, conference/convention facilities and additional accommodation facilities.
ANZ Securities' Webb said that, over time, development of Sky City's "land bank" had potential to create substantial shareholder value.
Guy Hallwright at First NZ Capital said slot revenues were stronger than expected, while table revenues were weaker. Overall, the result was slightly below expectations but not by much.
Last year brokers adjusted their earnings profiles downward after an enthusiastic debut on the share market in February, when the casino opened its doors.
Sky City was down 20 cents at NZ$7.00 in late trade.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746)
